title: Kavantissa was not just another elephant: Why Sri Lanka must rethink its wildlife conservation priorities | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 23 October 2026 02:56
-     - 7

The true measure of a nation’s commitment to wildlife conservation is not how deeply it mourns its iconic animals after they die, but how effectively it protects them while they are still alive

The death of Kavantissa on 16 October 2026 was a profound loss for Sri Lanka. One of the country’s most magnificent wild tuskers, he was estimated to be around 45 years old when he died, following several weeks of veterinary treatment for a reported gunshot injury. His death has prompted widespread grief, raised questions about the medical care he received and renewed calls for better protection of Sri Lanka’s remaining wild tuskers.

It has also exposed a disagreement about what conservation should mean in practice. Following Kavantissa’s death, the Director-General of Wildlife Conservation defended the Department’s holistic approach to elephant management rather than a focus on individual animals. Some elephant specialists make a similar argument: Sri Lanka must devote its limited resources to conserving the population as a whole and reducing human–elephant conflict (HEC), not to protecting a few well-known elephants.

But it does not follow that an elephant such as Kavantissa should receive no additional attention. Protecting a population and responding to the needs of an individual animal are not opposing ideas. The real question is whether a responsible wildlife authority should recognise differences in biological characteristics, exposure to danger and the likely benefit of intervention.

I believe it should. Equal concern for every elephant does not require precisely the same intervention for every elephant. That is not a sentimental argument. It is a matter of sound management.

Why the rarity of tuskers matters

Sri Lanka has an unusual feature within its wild elephant population: only a small proportion of adult males carry prominent tusks. In many other Asian elephant populations, the proportion is considerably higher, although it varies between places and over time.

A study by Fred Kurt, Günther Hartl and Ralph Tiedemann, published in Acta Theriologica in 1995, examined historical records and population genetics to investigate this difference. The researchers referred to estimates suggesting that about 93% of Sri Lanka's subadult and adult male elephants were tuskless. Their historical analysis and modelling indicated that selective capture and killing of tuskers may have played an important part in producing this pattern.

These are historical estimates, not figures from a recent elephant census. Nor has modern research fully resolved how tusk development is inherited in Asian elephants. There may be several influences on the prevalence of tusks, and we should be careful not to treat one historical explanation as the whole story.

Still, the study raises a question that deserves more attention than it has received. If human activities have helped reduce the occurrence of a natural characteristic over many generations, should we not investigate that change and take reasonable steps to prevent further avoidable losses?

Having tusks does not make a male elephant genetically superior, nor does it necessarily make him a more successful breeder. Research by Karpagam Chelliah and Raman Sukumar, published in Animal Behaviour in 2013, found that body size and musth, a periodic reproductive condition experienced by adult bulls, were generally more important than tusks in determining dominance during male encounters.

Tuskless males are essential members of the population and deserve the same fundamental protection. Indeed, emergency veterinary care should depend on the needs of the animal, not whether it happens to possess tusks or attract public attention.

But that is different from saying the rarity of tuskers has no conservation relevance. Conservation is not concerned only with preventing extinction. It also involves understanding the variation found within a population, how that variation has changed, and whether human pressures are causing it to disappear. Kavantissa stood out even among Sri Lanka's tuskers. His extraordinary stature and prominent tusks made him one of our most recognisable wild elephants. As a tusker, he also belonged to a relatively small proportion of Sri Lanka's wild male elephant population. These facts do not prove that his genes were more valuable than those of another elephant. They do give us a reason to ask whether his circumstances warranted closer assessment and preventive monitoring.

Kavantissa estimated age of around 45 has sometimes been compared with that of an elderly human being. However, such comparisons have no established scientific basis, as elephants age differently from humans. More importantly, our responsibility to protect wild elephants should not depend on their age, reproductive potential or perceived usefulness. Kavantissa's life was valuable in its own right, just as the lives of all other wild elephants are. His age should not diminish the responsibility to protect him from avoidable human-induced threats.

Protecting people and protecting elephants

No serious discussion about elephant conservation in Sri Lanka can ignore the suffering caused by human–elephant conflict. Families have lost breadwinners; farmers have watched their crops destroyed; children and older people in some villages live with the fear of an elephant encounter after dark.

A Reuters report published on 14 October 2026 stated that, since 2019, Sri Lanka has recorded annual averages of approximately 138 human deaths and 402 elephant deaths in the wider human–elephant conflict crisis. Behind every figure lies a loss that statistics alone cannot describe.

It would be wrong to ask rural communities to bear the costs of conserving elephants without providing effective protection for their lives, homes and livelihoods. Human safety must remain paramount, and reducing conflict must be a central responsibility of the State.

The National Action Plan for Human–Elephant Conflict Mitigation provides an important scientific starting point. It recognises that much of the elephants’ range is outside protected areas, where farming communities also live. Rather than trying to push all elephants into national parks, it calls for protecting settlements and cultivation through practical, locally appropriate measures.

The problem is not that the country has no scientific proposals. It is that implementation has too often failed to match the scale and urgency of the crisis.

Why, then, is better protection for vulnerable tuskers sometimes treated as a rival to HEC mitigation? The Department of Wildlife Conservation has several responsibilities. It must conserve habitats and populations, prevent illegal killing, respond to injuries and help communities live more safely alongside wildlife. These duties are connected, but they are not identical.

An elephant that frequently enters a dangerous settlement corridor may need different monitoring from one in a relatively secure part of a protected area. An injured elephant may require urgent clinical intervention. An identifiable tusker with a history of threats may justify additional preventive attention. None of this means other elephants matter less.

There is a genuine question of cost. Wildlife officers, vehicles, veterinary equipment and public funds are limited. Money spent on one animal must be justified against what that money could achieve elsewhere. Any special protection program that merely creates new titles, offices or publicity opportunities would be difficult to defend.

The answer is a modest, risk-based program working through existing field and HEC operations, rather than an expensive parallel institution. Where closer monitoring can warn communities of an approaching elephant, identify a hazardous location or allow earlier treatment of an injury, it may benefit people as well as wildlife. Those benefits must be measured, not simply asserted.

And one distinction must remain clear: preventive monitoring of a high-risk animal is not the same as giving it priority over others in emergency medical care. An unknown tuskless male suffering a serious injury should not receive poorer treatment because a famous tusker commands more public attention. Clinical decisions must be based on need, urgency, welfare and the realistic prospects of treatment.

A lesson from Kenya, not a model to copy blindly

The idea that an exceptional elephant may warrant additional protection has a long history. In Kenya, Ahmed, the celebrated tusker of Marsabit, became the subject of a campaign by schoolchildren concerned about his safety. 

In 1970 President Jomo Kenyatta placed him under presidential protection. Recognised as a living national monument, Ahmed was watched day and night by armed rangers until his death, reportedly from natural causes, in 1974.

The importance of this episode is not the ceremony surrounding a famous animal. Kenya acknowledged that a recognisable elephant with unusually large tusks faced a particular danger and took steps to protect him.

A more useful contemporary example is the Big Tusker Project in Kenya’s Tsavo Conservation Area. Tsavo Trust, working with the Kenya Wildlife Service, uses aerial surveillance, mobile field teams and individual identification to help protect exceptional elephants while supporting wider conservation work. The program was described by Moller, Cahill and Kimaile in a 2019 paper in the International Zoo Yearbook.

Kenya’s experience offers a useful precedent, but not a ready-made solution for Sri Lanka. Targeted protection can operate within a broader programme for habitats, wildlife and surrounding communities. However, this does not necessarily mean that the same methods would succeed in Sri Lanka or that the costs would be justified here.

The two countries face different threats. Large African tuskers are especially vulnerable to ivory poaching. Sri Lanka’s elephants face shootings, electrocutions, accidents, land-use pressures and the daily hazards of conflict with people living across elephant range.

We should therefore learn from Kenya’s principle, not copy its arrangements. We do not need armed escorts for every well-known tusker. We need to identify our own risks and decide, on evidence, when additional protection is likely to prevent harm.

Could more have been done for Kavantissa?

Kavantissa’s final weeks deserve careful, independent scrutiny. According to the account given by the Department of Wildlife Conservation and reported in The Sunday Times on 18 October, veterinary officers attended to him after receiving information about a reported shooting in September. Treatment was provided, two teams were assigned to observe his condition, and additional specialists were consulted when his health deteriorated.

Those efforts should be recognised. Wildlife veterinarians and field officers often work long hours in dangerous and difficult circumstances. It would be unfair to question their professional dedication without evidence. But the commitment of individual officers is not the same thing as the effectiveness of the institution around them. We need to examine what happened before the injury as carefully as what happened afterwards.

Was Kavantissa known to face particular risks in the areas he frequented? Had those risks been assessed? Could preventive monitoring or better coordination with communities have reduced his exposure? 

Once he was injured, were the necessary diagnostic facilities, specialist advice, transport and clinical resources available at the right time? Could a different response have altered the outcome?

These are questions for an investigation, not conclusions that can responsibly be drawn from his death alone. We cannot yet say that negligence caused the loss of Kavantissa, or that better monitoring would certainly have saved him. Equally, the provision of treatment does not, by itself, settle whether the wider system was adequate.

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake has appointed an expert committee to examine the immediate and underlying causes of Kavantissa’s death, consider possible lapses in his treatment and recommend procedures for wild elephant welfare and a national conservation program. Its mandate is sufficiently broad to look beyond the final clinical episode.

The committee should seek the expertise it needs and distinguish clinical findings from shortcomings in policy, equipment or field coordination. 

Its report should be published, subject to legitimate investigative restrictions, and accompanied by responsibility for implementing its recommendations.

Sri Lanka has established many committees over the years. Public confidence will depend less on the announcement of another inquiry than on what changes after its findings are delivered.

A practical way forward for Sri Lanka’s remaining tuskers

Sri Lanka should establish a scientifically designed, risk-based program for vulnerable wild elephants, with a specific component addressing the remaining wild tuskers. This would sit within the Department of Wildlife Conservation and work closely with its HEC mitigation and veterinary services, rather than competing with them.

The starting point should be reliable information. The Department, working with researchers and experienced field observers, could maintain a regularly updated register of identifiable tuskers, using photographs, observations and relevant health records. It would document broad ranges, past injuries and known threats, while keeping precise location data secure so that the exercise does not itself increase the risk of harm.

Additional monitoring should then follow clear criteria: evidence of repeated threats, exposure to conflict, an animal’s vulnerability, the feasibility of intervention and the likely benefit to wildlife and nearby communities. Fame alone should not qualify an animal for special treatment.

Technology has a role, but it is not a substitute for field judgment. GPS collars may help in selected cases, although immobilisation, collaring and continuing maintenance bring financial and animal-welfare costs. Routine observation, photographic identification, responsible community reporting and better communication between local wildlife teams may sometimes achieve more with fewer risks.

Our veterinary response also needs attention. Field officers should have dependable access to appropriate diagnostic equipment, mobile treatment facilities, specialist consultation and clear emergency protocols. These investments would improve care for all injured wild elephants, not just the most recognisable tuskers.

A pilot program could begin in a limited number of high-risk landscapes with a published budget and clear objectives. 

Independent evaluation should examine whether it improves the detection of threats, shortens response times, reduces avoidable injuries or helps prevent dangerous encounters with people. The scheme should be expanded only when the evidence warrants it.

At the same time, Sri Lanka needs updated research on the proportion of tusked males, tusk inheritance and the effects of selective mortality on the population. We should not continue relying on historical estimates when contemporary scientific methods could provide a better basis for decisions.

None of this requires making elephants dependent on human attention. Wild elephants must remain wild. Interventions should be limited to what is reasonably necessary to reduce avoidable human-induced harm, without encouraging habituation, dangerous close contact or unnecessary disturbance.

Ultimately, success should be judged by fewer preventable injuries, safer communities and better conservation outcomes, not simply by the number of meetings, patrols or collars.

The legacy Kavantissa deserves

What concerns me about the debate following Kavantissa ’s death is the suggestion that caring about an individual animal is somehow at odds with scientific conservation. It need not be. 

Science should help us understand why particular animals face particular risks and how we can respond without neglecting the population or the people who share its landscape.

Public grief cannot be a substitute for evidence. But scientific authority should not be used to brush aside legitimate questions from the public. When an animal as remarkable as Kavantissa  dies, people are entitled to ask whether our institutions did all that could reasonably have been done and what they will do differently next time.

The Department of Wildlife Conservation exists not merely to administer land and respond to emergencies, but to protect the country’s wildlife for future generations. That requires sound science, experienced field staff, capable leadership, adequate resources and accountability for conservation outcomes.

Kavantissa  was not more entitled to live than another elephant. Yet he was not indistinguishable from every other elephant either. He belonged to a relatively uncommon group, possessed extraordinary physical characteristics and had become a symbol of Sri Lanka’s natural heritage. Recognising those facts does not diminish other elephants or the communities who must be protected from conflict.

The argument should no longer be about whether one famous tusker deserved attention. It should be about whether Sri Lanka has the capacity to identify foreseeable risks early, protect people effectively and prevent avoidable losses among the elephants that remain.

We do not need another conservation program that exists only on paper. We need better implementation of HEC mitigation, stronger veterinary preparedness, practical monitoring of vulnerable animals and transparent institutional accountability. Above all, we must shift from responding to tragedies towards preventing them wherever reasonably possible.

The true measure of a nation’s commitment to wildlife conservation is not how deeply it mourns its iconic animals after they die, but how effectively it protects them while they are still alive.

(The author is a telecommunications engineer turned environmental and wildlife conservationist, citizen scientist and wildlife documentary filmmaker. His work bridges science, public policy and sustainable development, with particular emphasis on the long-term conservation of Sri Lanka’s elephants and other threatened species)

title: Sri Lanka beat England  in phenomenal run chase | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 23 October 2026 02:32
-     - 7

RAWALPINDI: What a game it turned out to be! Chasing 430 was always going to be a monumental task, but Sri Lanka pulled off the unthinkable beating England by two wickets with a ball to spare to register their first win in the Pakistan ODI Tri-Series at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium yesterday.

This incredible chase had to rank among the greatest run chases of all time! South Africa’s famous chase of 434 set the benchmark, and now Sri Lanka produced something equally extraordinary - an absolutely phenomenal effort.

Earlier in the day, Harry Brook lit up the contest with the fastest double century in ODI history, powering England to their highest-ever total in the format. But in a remarkable turn of events, Sri Lanka managed to outdo even that extraordinary feat with a sensational run chase.

Avishka Fernando provided the perfect launch pad with a blistering 97 off 83 balls (11 fours, 2 sixes) at the top of the order, and Pavan Rathnayake chipped in with a magnificent century – 130 off 106 balls (15 fours, 3 sixes) to lay the foundation for Sri Lanka’s record run chase. The pair put on 166 off 137 balls for the third wicket after Kamindu Mendis was out for 18 and skipper Kusal Mendis run out at the non-striker’s end without facing a ball.

Dasun Shanaka promoted in the batting to no. 5 hit an explosive 97 off just 50 deliveries (6 fours, 8 sixes) and that truly swung the momentum in Sri Lanka’s favour, turning an already remarkable chase into something truly unbelievable.

Shanaka, like Fernando, fell agonisingly short of a century, but Janith Liyanage rose to the occasion with a career-defining knock (61* off 27 balls, 7 fours, 3 sixes), holding his nerve to steer Sri Lanka home in a thrilling finish in the final over. Josh Tongue’s double strike in the final over briefly threatened to turn the game on its head, but Liyanage held his nerve under immense pressure, delivering when Sri Lanka needed him the most, finishing the match in style with a straight six.

Earlier, England put into bat first hit up a colossal total of 429-4, giving their bowlers a huge cushion to work with. England’s openers laid a solid foundation with an impressive partnership at the top, with Tom Banton scoring a 50 off 51 balls (9 fours). However, it was the crucial stand of 159 off 127 balls between Joe Root and Harry Brook that firmly put England in the driver’s seat.


Brook delivered a breathtaking knock of 202 off 116 balls (21 fours, 10 sixes), tearing into the Sri Lankan attack as the bowlers struggled to find answers to his relentless onslaught. He lit up Rawalpindi with a dazzling array of attacking strokes, keeping the spectators entertained with his explosive shot-making throughout the innings.Brook became the first England batsman to score a double ton in ODIs, and it was also the quickest double ton in ODIs by a batsman off 114 balls beating the previous best off 117 balls by Shubman Gill for India against West Indies at Guwahati this year.

Joe Root (69 off 66 balls, 8 fours) and Will Jacks (66* off 30 balls, 8 fours, 3 sixes) played valuable supporting roles, forging crucial partnerships with their Captain to put England ahead in the contest. Jacks helped Brooks add 185 off 77 balls as England scored 156 off the final 10 overs. Dunith Wellalage managed to pick up a couple of wickets, but the rest of the Sri Lankan attack struggled to contain Brook and company, with most of the bowlers proving costly.

title: Palitha Bandara wins Silver as Naveed Rahim and Maduranga secure Bronze | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 23 October 2026 02:27
-     - 14

By Hishan Welmilla

Aichi-Nagoya: Sri Lanka enjoyed a memorable day at the 5th Asian Para Games 2026, with Palitha Bandara winning a Silver medal in the men’s F42 shot put and swimmer Naveed Rahim claiming Bronze in the men’s S9 100m butterfly. Meanwhile, Maduranga Subasinghe delivered a season-best performance in the men’s T47 400m final and secured a Bronze after the technical committee evaluation found he and Uzbekistan’s Marufojon Morodollove finished third with equal timing.

Palitha Bandara secured Sri Lanka’s silver medal in the men’s F42 shot put with an impressive throw of 14.02 metres, earning a place on the podium at the continental competition.

Kuwait’s Faizal Sorsour won the gold medal with a Games-record throw of 16.06 metres, setting a new benchmark in the event. Bandara’s performance, meanwhile, added another significant achievement to his para-athletics career and reinforced his position among Asia’s leading competitors in the discipline.

Bandara had previously won a bronze medal at the 2023 Asian Para Games with a throw of 14.15 metres. His latest podium finish represents another important milestone in his long-standing career in para-athletics.

Sri Lanka’s medal celebrations continued in the swimming pool, where Naveed Rahim captured the bronze medal in the men’s S9 100m butterfly, clocking an impressive 1:03.29 in the final.

Rahim’s medal-winning performance marked an outstanding achievement for the Sri Lankan swimmer, who had demonstrated his potential during the qualifying rounds. He secured his place in the final with a personal-best time of 1:05.55, underlining his progress and determination ahead of the medal-deciding race.

His improvement in the final culminated in a podium finish, providing Sri Lanka with another valuable medal at the Games.

At the 2023 Para Asian Games held in Hangzhou, China, he secured the bronze in the Men’s 400m Freestyle (S9) event with a time of 4:39.63, breaking a 13-year dry spell for Sri Lanka in Para Asian Games swimming.

Sri Lankan swimmer Galina Basnayake finished seventh in the women’s S9 100m butterfly. She recorded a time of 1:21.98 in a competitive field, gaining further experience at the prestigious continental event despite missing out on a medal.

On the athletics track, Maduranga Subasinghe secured the Bronze finishing equally on third place with Uzbekistan’s Marufojon Morodollove.

Subasinghe had qualified for the final after clocking 51.31 seconds in his heat, demonstrating his ability to compete among the leading athletes in his classification. He improved his time significantly in the final, producing a determined performance reflecting his commitment to continued improvement at the highest level of competition.

Sri Lankan para-athlete Nuwan Indika finished fourth in the men’s T44 long jump at the 5th Asian Para Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, recording a distance of 6.30 metres. The result marked a disappointing outcome for Indika, who had enjoyed a successful campaign at the 2023 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou, China, where he won the silver medal in the men’s long jump with a leap of 6.68 metres and also claimed gold in the men’s T44 100m with a Games-record time of 11.63 seconds.

Sri Lanka’s performances across athletics and swimming highlighted the determination and competitive spirit of the country’s para-athletes at the 5th Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. Bandara’s silver and Rahim’s bronze provided important additions to the national medal tally, while the performances of Basnayake and Subasinghe demonstrated the depth of Sri Lanka’s participation across different events.

As the competition continues, Sri Lanka’s athletes will look to build on these achievements and pursue further success on the Asian stage.

title: SLC awards certificates to 51 Level 5 umpires | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 23 October 2026 02:24
-     - 7

Former ICC Elite Panel Umpire Asoka de Silva presents a certificate to one of the participants

SLC Senior Manager - Umpire Development Lyndon Hannibal presents a certificate to one of the participants

Sri Lanka Cricket awarded certificates to 51 newly qualified umpires who passed the Level 5 examination, the entry-level qualification for umpiring in Sri Lanka.

The group comprised 47 males and four female umpires, who will now have the opportunity to officiate at District and Provincial tournaments organized by Sri Lanka Cricket.

Their addition forms part of Sri Lanka Cricket’s ongoing efforts to ensure an adequate number of match officials are available to officiate at School, District, Provincial level competitions.

The newly qualified umpires have entered a development pathway that offers opportunities to progress towards international umpiring, based on their commitment and performance.

Beginning at Level 5, umpires can advance through Levels 4, 3 and 2 before progressing to First-Class status.

Sri Lanka Cricket regularly maintains a 20-member First-Class Umpiring Panel that serves as the pool from which umpires are nominated for consideration for the ICC International Panel of Umpires.

The award ceremony took place recently at Sri Lanka Cricket headquarters with the participation of Asoka de Silva, a former Sri Lanka cricketer and former ICC Elite Panel umpire who currently serves on the Domestic Cricket Committee, and Lyndon Hannibal, a former ICC umpire who currently serves as Sri Lanka Cricket’s Senior Manager, Umpire Development.

Her attention now turns to the long jump, where she will have another opportunity to showcase her athletic ability and fight for a strong finish. The experience gained from both the 200m success and the closely contested 100m final could prove valuable as she prepares for her next challenge.

title: Sri Lanka showcases over 90 local brands at SIAL Paris 2026 | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 23 October 2026 02:43
-     - 2

Strong national participation, award-winning innovation, and buyer engagement marked Sri Lanka’s presence at Salon International de l’Alimentation (SIAL Paris 2026), the world’s leading international food industry exhibition, held in Paris from 17 to 21 October. 

Supported by the Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB), the Sri Lanka Tea Board, and the Embassy of Sri Lanka in France, 92 companies participated, creating valuable opportunities to promote Sri Lankan products and strengthen international business links.

The 2026 edition of the world-leading food exhibition reached a historic scale, bringing together 8,000 exhibitors from 127 countries and attracting more than 295,000 trade professionals worldwide.

Sri Lanka’s participation advanced the country’s national export-promotion goals. The delegation comprised 92 companies: 64 major exporters, 20 exhibitors in the EDB pavilion, and 8 companies in the Sri Lanka Tea Board pavilion. 

The national pavilions were officially inaugurated on 17 October 2026 with a ceremonial ribbon-cutting by Sri Lanka’s Ambassador to France, Sugeeshwara Gunaratna. Throughout the five-day fair, First Secretary (Commercial) Prasadi Boomawalage and Embassy officials provided hands-on support and facilitated business-to-business engagement. 

To attract international buyers, the EDB pavilion hosted daily live culinary demonstrations. Leading chefs created recipes using value-added Sri Lankan products, premium spices, and Pure Ceylon Tea, demonstrating how readily these ingredients can meet contemporary global gourmet demands. 

The National Organic Control Unit (NOCU) of the EDB was also represented at the fair to raise awareness of the Sri Lankan National Organic Certificate and the country’s organic products among potential international buyers. 

Four participating Sri Lankan companies received SIAL 2026 Recognition & Innovation Awards, providing strong international recognition for the country’s product development and value-added offerings: Dilmah - Non-Alcoholic Sparkling Tea Collection; Russell’s Global - Wellness Tea; CinZ - Ready-to-Drink Cinnamon Concentrate and Goodness Factory - Premium Rice Bran Oil.

The Embassy also utilised the event to invite prospective buyers to Sri Lanka Expo 2027, scheduled to take place in Colombo from 14 to 17 January 2027.

title: Hunas Hospitality launches unified brand with opening of Hunas Beach | Daily FT

Hunas Hospitality has launched its unified hospitality brand alongside the opening of Hunas Beach on 17 October in the Southern Coast of Balapitiya, marking a strategic expansion of its portfolio and bringing its Sri Lankan leadership and Japanese partners together under a common growth vision.

Building on the established Hunas Falls brand, the group is expanding beyond the hill country into coastal hospitality, with a riverside property planned as the next addition to its portfolio. The strategy aims to build a diversified collection of destinations under one brand, strengthening its market presence in Sri Lanka’s tourism and hospitality sector.

Hunas Hospitality Managing Director Atheeq Ansar said the launch builds on the Hunas legacy, bringing together a shared Sri Lankan and Japanese vision for distinctive hospitality experiences.

“This evening is not simply the celebration of one hotel; it marks the beginning of many more exciting projects and opportunities that we look forward to bringing to life together, under one unified brand which is Hunas Hospitality,” he said.

Ansar acknowledged the contribution of the group’s Japanese partners and the enduring relationships that have helped bring the shared vision to life.

Japanese director Watanabe-san reflected on his first investment in Sri Lanka 13 years ago, recalling the country’s promise and expressing his continued confidence in its future.

“We are looking forward to growing together and building something meaningful in Sri Lanka’s tourism and hospitality industry,” he said.

He also highlighted the warmth of Sri Lankan hospitality as one of the country’s defining strengths, noting that the genuine welcome and personal care extended to guests set the country apart.

Rajith Gooneratne, Head of Hunas Hospitality, said the unified brand would extend the spirit of Hunas beyond the hills, bringing distinctive destinations together under a shared vision of elevating hospitality and connecting extraordinary experiences.

With the opening of Hunas Beach, which offers 26 luxury rooms, all facing the sea, with private balconies. the group is extending its hospitality offering to the coast, with plans to develop a portfolio spanning hill-country, coastal and riverside destinations.

The property will also feature an all-day dining restaurant, a beachside specialty cocktail bar and a range of other high-end facilities.

The group said its approach would be guided by genuine warmth, a strong sense of place, thoughtful service and a commitment to sustainable growth, as it seeks to build on the legacy of Hunas Falls and strengthen its presence in Sri Lanka’s tourism and hospitality sector.

Hunas Hospitality brings together distinctive Sri Lankan hospitality experiences under one unified brand.

title: Sri Lanka Embassy in Belgium partners Emirates, Jetwing Travels for exclusive tourism showcase | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 23 October 2026 02:38
-     - 4

The Embassy of Sri Lanka in Belgium, in collaboration with Emirates and Jetwing Travels Sri Lanka, hosted an exclusive tourism showcase titled “An Evening in Ceylon” on 13 October 2026 at the Sri Lanka Residence in Brussels. 

Over 50 prominent tourism industry representatives, travel trade professionals, and distinguished guests attended the event. The initiative served as a strategic platform to enhance destination awareness and build stronger tourism links between Sri Lanka and the Belgian market. 

Adding special prestige to the occasion, the Parliament Speaker Dr. Jagath Wickramaratne, who was in Brussels on an official visit, attended as the special guest. In his address, he emphasised Sri Lanka’s enduring appeal, warm hospitality, and vast array of attractions, which make the island an unforgettable destination for tourists worldwide.

Ambassador Chandana Weerasena in his speech explained how Sri Lanka is distinct among many other destinations because of its unrivalled combination of wild life and nature and cultural heritage. Emirates Country Manager for Belgium and Luxembourg, Jean-Pierre Martin highlighted Emirates’ valued partnership in promoting Sri Lanka as a travel destination. 

Jetwing Travels Director Bandula Withana explained a longstanding role of the company in promoting Sri Lanka through its tour operations association with Jetwing Hotels, which offers a collection of eco-luxury hospitality properties across the island.

Jetwing Travels Business Development Manager of BENELUX and DACH Lieke Schroeder presented Sri Lanka’s tourism experiences and the company’s destination management services highlighting the range of experiences available in Sri Lanka to international visitors, encompassing Sri Lanka’s natural landscapes, cultural heritage and hospitality.

Emirates Belgium Sales Executive Laurent Meulewaeter presented the airline’s services and connectivity to Sri Lanka highlighting the importance of air connectivity in facilitating travel and supporting tourism links between Belgium and Sri Lanka.

The event provided guests with an opportunity to learn about diverse tourism offerings in Sri Lanka while experiencing distinctive aspects of Sri Lankan culture and true hospitality through authentic Sri Lankan traditional culinary specialties and beverages and wearing traditional clothes. A live hopper station and cocktail prepared with Sri Lankan traditional beverage were arranged to offer a real authentic Sri Lankan flavours to the participants. Guests were presented with traditional Sri Lankan sarongs to wear during the evening and this thoughtful gesture was warmly appreciated and attracted by the guests.

The evening concluded with a quiz competition. Two lucky winners each received an Economy Class return ticket to Sri Lanka, courtesy of Emirates, together with a complete land package in Sri Lanka provided by Jetwing Travels. Two additional winners received complete land packages courtesy of Jetwing Travels. The prizes will offer winners an opportunity to experience Sri Lanka’s attractions and hospitality first-hand.

The event was organised as a part of the Embassy’s ongoing efforts to promote Sri Lanka as a destination for tourism, cultural discovery, nature-based experiences and authentic hospitality. Through continued cooperation with airlines, destination management companies and tourism industry stakeholders, the Embassy seeks to strengthen Sri Lanka’s visibility in Belgium, deepen engagement with the local travel trade and encourage further growth in tourist arrivals to Sri Lanka from Europe.
